hints.hint: Name the unknowns and turn every condition, including a remark about what someone knows, into an explicit constraint: an equation, a divisibility, an inequality, a bound. Impose them in the given order, and apply each constraint to BOTH members of a pair, not just one: mutual requirements are severe and often force the symmetric case where the two unknowns coincide, so test that case early instead of only enumerating lopsided ones. Integrality plus a bound beats searching. Re-read what is asked and report that quantity, not a partner you solved for on the way. A contradiction is a deduction: it kills one assumption you added, usually knowledge you granted someone. Name which died and move on; never call the problem broken and never report a value you already refuted. State your result before you run long, verify once, stop.
hints.mutation: impose every constraint on both members of the pair so the symmetric equal-unknowns case surfaces early, and add a re-read-what-is-asked guard against reporting the partner value
hints.subagent_summary: Fresh sampling with the incumbent scored 1/8; two rollouts died at the 16384 cap and all eight burned 14k-16.4k tokens. Six failures fixed one reading of the shown number, enumerated its factor pairs, proved a speaker's own value pins the partner, then declared a contradiction and reported a factor their own text had just refuted; two also reported the partner rather than the quantity actually asked for. The single success was the one rollout that reasoned about the symmetric split where both unknowns coincide, a candidate no factor enumeration reaches. The incumbent's intersect-across-live-readings clause never fires because the budget is gone first, so I replaced it with two cheaper levers it has never had together: impose every constraint on both members of the pair so the symmetric case surfaces early, and re-check which quantity is actually requested before reporting.

hints.hint:
Divide by the appropriate power of the variable to introduce the ratio w=(z-1)/z; the equation then pins w to a finite set on a circle. Solve for z in terms of w and turn the locus into an equation in x and y, completing the square to read off center and radius. Generally: substitute so the relation depends on one quantity, and keep every value exact.

Compute the two or three easiest exact instances first: the real ones, or wherever a parameter takes its simplest value. They are cheap, they reveal the shape of the object you want, and with symmetry they pin it without any large linear system. Anchor your general result to them. If a messier instance clashes, the slip is in that instance's arithmetic, not the setup: redo that line, never restart. Write your simplified value down as soon as you have one.
hints.mutation: make the easiest exact instances plus symmetry the primary constructive tool for pinning the requested object, replacing the round-14 magnitude-plausibility check clause
hints.subagent_summary: 7 of 8 fresh rollouts were correct in 5.8k-9.1k tokens. The failure reached the correct locus and radius by ~3k tokens, then spot-checked a messy complex root, mis-inverted a purely imaginary reciprocal so its modulus grew instead of shrinking, and spent the remaining 13k tokens re-auditing a sound derivation until the cap with nothing recorded. Rounds 5-14 all tried to bound, reorder or repair that audit loop and every one lost transfer, while the only proposal that ever raised transfer carried concrete constructive machinery. So I make cheap exact instances the primary tool rather than a late check: compute the easiest ones (the real ones, where signs and reciprocals cannot bite), let them plus symmetry pin the object without a large linear system, and anchor the general result to them.

hints.hint: Fix one setup and never rebuild it. Overlapping pieces obey total = sum minus overlap, so maximize coverage by minimizing overlap; the same bookkeeping serves counting. A corner reaches only the directions inside its own angle, so what it covers of the small piece is a wedge: part of that piece always lies outside, part always inside. The overlap is therefore strictly between zero and the whole piece; both extreme claims are wrong. Settle the free parameter by a trade, not by sampling: shift it slightly and compare what enters the overlap against what leaves. Matched pieces mean the quantity never moved, so no further value can teach you anything. End reasoning there, do the sum-minus-overlap arithmetic in your first visible line, and state the result next. Never append a section asking whether another configuration wins.
hints.mutation: make the wedge caution two-sided (overlap is strictly partial, so neither containment nor zero overlap), replace parameter sampling with a local enters-vs-leaves trade test, and ban the trailing 'is another configuration better' section that eats the write-up
hints.subagent_summary: Only 2 of 8 scored. No failure was mathematical: 6 of 8 held the right overlap value inside the first 3-7k of ~52-62k characters, then spent 98-182 rotation re-tests and 45-83 restarts. Four never closed reasoning at all, oscillating between two wrong extremes - that the big square contains the small one entirely, or that tilting could remove overlap - and one explicitly quoted the incumbent's one-sided wedge clause and concluded containment. Two closed reasoning but were truncated inside a trailing optimality-check section that re-litigated rotation instead of reporting. So this revision makes the wedge bound two-sided (overlap is a proper part, so both extremes are wrong), swaps abstract 'don't sample' for a concrete local trade test comparing what enters against what leaves, and forbids the trailing better-configuration section.

hints.hint:
For "at most how many" questions give both halves: a bound and an example reaching it. Name a count early.

Posit ONE unknown affine target for the whole pattern (an arithmetic progression is A+B*n), shared by every piece. Index n suits piece f exactly when the residual f(x)-(A+Bx) vanishes at n. Never demand one piece alone give consecutive terms; neighbours may come from different pieces.

Reuse is unrestricted unless forbidden - but that does NOT make the count unbounded, and it does not make pieces single-use either. Both of those dead ends end at the bare piece count m; refuse it.

Per piece the cap is d, the degree handed to you verbatim: a degree-d curve meeting a line more often would BE that line. Never d-1. Budgets ADD: m*d.

Attain it with consecutive blocks, one piece each.
hints.mutation: name the unbounded/single-use pair as one dead end ending at the piece count, and pin the per-piece cap to the stated degree verbatim by an agreement argument
hints.subagent_summary: Fresh 8 rollouts with the incumbent scored 3/8. The failures cluster on two distinct routes that both terminate at the bare piece count: two argued each piece is single-use (one after first declaring the count unbounded because reuse is allowed, then retreating), and both reported m. The other two computed the per-piece cap one below the stated degree and reported m*(d-1). One long rollout truncated while forcing a single piece to step by the common difference. So the incumbent's residual-degree audit is feeding the off-by-one rather than fixing it. The revision names the unbounded-then-single-use trap explicitly as the same dead end, pins the per-piece cap to the degree given verbatim via an agreement argument instead of a subtract-then-degree step, and keeps the shared-affine-target framing that all three successes used.

hints.hint: Name your unknowns and turn each given condition into one exact equation; solve for any constants first. Reduce to a single variable, keep exact fractions, and discard roots that are degenerate or outside the domain. A root that merely reproduces data you were already handed is likewise an artifact of your own setup, not the object asked about, so take the other one. Verify with a second, different method rather than repeating the first. State your result early, then stop.
hints.mutation: append artifact-root criterion (a root reproducing given data is a setup artifact) alongside the retained domain check
hints.subagent_summary: 7 of 8 fresh rollouts were correct. The lone failure derived both roots of the reduced quadratic, and both were genuinely inside the domain, but it kept only the root that reproduced the two points it had already been handed. That forced a degenerate figure and a zero value, which it then rationalized for thousands of tokens instead of revisiting the other root. Round 11 tested exactly this artifact-root rule and produced the best transfer this hint has seen, but it deleted the out-of-domain clause and train collapsed. So this revision is purely additive: the incumbent is preserved verbatim and the artifact-root criterion is appended as an extra screen alongside the domain check rather than replacing it.

hints.hint:
Randomness in the STEPS rarely gives uniformity over OUTCOMES, so 1/n and 1/n! are guesses. Price steps by walking the process: 1/2 only where both options are legal, 1 where a side is empty or exhausted.

Then attack the wording of the asked position, where most attempts die. Never restate a position by WHEN something was handled. Things are placed ON TOP of what is already there, so the DEEPEST slot holds the EARLIEST arrival, never the item handled last. Verify that by running one concrete instance and writing the result out in arrival order.

Which item reaches the deepest slot is therefore settled by the OPENING steps, not the closing ones: name the exact opening run that forces it and pay 1/2 per free step inside.

Use the smallest case where the question still makes sense, and take method from it, not its value. Parts may share a value.
hints.mutation: make the position-to-time mapping the centerpiece: forbid rewording a position as a timing, verify orientation on one concrete run, and count the opening steps instead of the closing ones
hints.subagent_summary: Fresh sampling with the incumbent gave 1/8; six rollouts finished early, so length is not the limit. Almost every failure came from one substitution: the asked deepest position was silently reworded as 'whatever was handled last', after which the student priced it as 1/n (or 1/2) by assumed symmetry. The incumbent states the arrival-order fact only in passing and buries it in abstract atom-counting, so it gets skipped. This revision makes the position-to-time mapping the centerpiece: forbid restating a position by timing, assert that the deepest slot is the earliest arrival, demand one concrete instance written in arrival order as a check, and redirect counting to the opening steps rather than the closing ones. It also blocks the degenerate tiny-case loop that stalled two rollouts into the token cap.

hints.hint: Reach a stated result early, then spend the rest of your effort checking it: reasoning that never lands scores nothing. At a large or symbolic size, work the smallest instances out exactly and substitute back to confirm each. Build that miniature to mirror the original: the same pattern of conditions, and exactly as many conditions as unknowns. If it comes out inconsistent or slack, you miscounted -- repair the count and re-solve. Never decide the small case is unlike the stated problem and walk away; that distrust strands you in symbolic algebra you cannot close. Read confirmed values by ratio as well as difference, since a ratio like 1/k exposes a factorial the raw list hides; watch sign and any off-by-one shift. Confirmed numbers are the route you finish: if one breaks a pattern the rest obey, recheck its arithmetic rather than retheorizing.
hints.mutation: make the small-case route survivable: mirror the original condition pattern with a matched count, treat an inconsistent miniature as a miscount to repair rather than a reason to distrust small cases, and read the confirmed list by ratio to expose factorial growth
hints.subagent_summary: Fresh sampling under the incumbent scored 0 of 8, with 7 of 8 hitting the token cap. The hint did get every rollout to try small instances, but each built the miniature wrong -- too many or too few vanishing conditions -- got a contradiction or a value that clashed with its own general form, and then concluded the small case was unlike the stated problem. All of them abandoned the concrete route there and sank the remaining budget into an unclosable symbolic expansion carrying a parameter the conditions never pinned; the two that emitted anything guessed. So the incumbent already commands the right route but leaves the reduction unspecified, and one bad miniature discredits the whole method. The revision specifies how to size and shape the miniature, reframes inconsistency as a miscount to repair, and adds ratio-reading so factorial growth is visible from few entries.

hints.hint: Let H be the total number of houses. The equal-street layout constrains H arithmetically, and integer stage costs per house mean H must divide every listed stage total. Determine the admissible common divisors using the intended maximum-feasible-count interpretation. Add all construction costs before dividing by H, and apply the stated markup multiplicatively. In general, reason backwards from the goal instead of forward from the givens: name the exact quantity wanted, ask what single fact would determine it, and chase only that fact. When a direct attack stalls, work the smallest cases by hand and read off the pattern or invariant rather than pushing a long computation. Keep quantities exact as fractions or products and simplify only at the close. State your result plainly as soon as you have it, then check it once.
hints.mutation: replace exact-fractions clause with untried backward/goal-directed reasoning rule (name target, find the one determining fact, chase only that chain)
hints.subagent_summary: All 8 fresh rollouts scored 1 (train saturated at 1.0 for the ninth straight round), so every remaining gain must come from transfer. The rollouts show no strategy or arithmetic failure: the student reaches the value within roughly 2k tokens, then burns 1k-19k more tokens re-litigating which admissible divisor is intended, repeatedly recomputing the same alternatives and asking whether information is missing. Prior rounds already tried scope-labeling, multiply-back, exact-fractions, output-form, case-uniqueness and arithmetic-reliability clauses; all lost transfer ground. So I keep the train-safe opening verbatim and swap the never-exercised exact-arithmetic advice for an untried goal-directed search rule: name the target quantity, ask what single fact determines it, and chase only that chain instead of expanding forward from the givens. That directly attacks the observed forward-exploration rumination and is broadly reusable.

hints.hint: Let your first written line be a structured form, never general unknown coefficients. For a condition holding for all x, never open by comparing leading coefficients or expanding a composition; that alone burns your budget. Write the smallest family satisfying the condition identically, then fit the data. For two same-degree maps that commute, that family shares one center c and carries the same odd-power term, added in one map and subtracted in the other, so the identity collapses by itself. The supplied values then sit symmetrically about c: adding them cancels that term and pins c, subtracting isolates the scale. Once both are pinned you are finished; read requested inputs off the centered form, never a re-expanded one. A failing spot-check is your own expansion slip, not refutation of the structure, and never a reason to discard a value already derived. Keep values exact, commit early, stop.
hints.mutation: ban the leading-coefficient-comparison opening (not just full expansion) and redirect the abort guard at re-expansion spot-checks, forbidding discard of an already-derived value
hints.subagent_summary: Fresh rollouts: 7/8 correct, so the centered recipe works when adopted. The single failure never wrote the centered form at all: it opened with eight general coefficients and a leading-coefficient comparison, then spent all 16384 tokens factoring cubics. Across prior rounds the other recurring loss is the opposite exit: the student derives the pair correctly, then re-expands into standard powers for a numeric spot-check, mis-expands, sees a mismatch, and abandons a value it had already obtained. So this revision makes the ban cover the leading-coefficient opening explicitly (previously only full expansion was banned), and reframes the abort guard around the real trigger: a failed spot-check is an expansion slip and is never grounds to discard a derived value or return to coefficients.

hints.hint: A repetitions-to-return count is an order, and no candidate is settled until the cheapest rival is refuted by an actual trace. Spend your budget refuting, not on cycle vocabulary. At the smallest non-degenerate size write distinct labels and rewrite the whole row after each listed step, each step acting on the row above, never on the original. Then run the cheap rival explicitly: apply the entire process a second time. If that does not restore the row, order two is dead; do not blame your trace or hunt a lost bookkeeping slip. "Disjoint swaps, so two passes undo it" is a conjecture about a product you never carried out, and so is any cycle length you did not walk. Expect the count to grow with the size of the object, not the step count. Trace two sizes, fit one formula, state your result early, stop.
hints.mutation: make explicit refutation of the cheap rival (run a second full pass) the required step, and rule that a failed second pass kills order-two outright instead of triggering a trace re-audit
hints.subagent_summary: Only 1 of 8 rollouts was correct. Seven failures all collapsed to the same move: the student called the composite a product of disjoint transpositions and read order two off that vocabulary without ever applying the whole process a second time. Three committed to 2, one to a per-size piecewise mess, one to a smaller power, and two burned the token cap re-auditing a single pass looking for a bookkeeping error that was not there. The incumbent already warned that swap-shaped stages need not have period 2, but a warning was not enough; nothing forced a test. The revision replaces the warning with a concrete refutation step: apply the entire process a second time, and treat a non-return as killing order two rather than as evidence the trace is wrong.
